24.11: 24.11 By the well. GREGORY. He stood by the fountain, and from a fixed sentence proposed what was to be chosen, because holy preachers consider the flowing words. Hence they gather whom, or in what hearers, they may take the confidence of certainty.
24.14: 24.14 Now the maid, etc. AUGUSTINE, Questions on Genesis. It is to be asked how unlawful auguries differ from this petition, etc., down to by which tempting God is forbidden. Incline your pitcher. Humble worldly eloquence to draw the prophetic speech, that you may incline your will to my persuasion.
24.17: 24.17 And the servant ran to meet her, and said: Give me a little water, etc. GREGORY. Allegorically. Every preacher thirsts for the soul of the hearer, therefore the servant asks, Rebecca gives drink: because the Church of the elect satisfies the desire of the preachers by the power of her faith. For she who confesses the God she hears offers the preacher the water of refreshment and cooling. And it is to be noted that she let down the pitcher from her shoulder, because that confession is pleasing which proceeds from a good work. Or she offered water, because in what she believed she did not remain empty. For she soon preached what she heard, and by speaking brought forth many preachers from herself. The water in the pitcher is the knowledge of preaching in due measure. For she takes care not to know more than it behooves to know. The pitcher on the arm is the measure of preaching in work. And she gives drink not only to all his companions, but to the camels too, because the word of life is preached not only to the prudent but also to the foolish. Romans 1: I am a debtor to the wise and to the unwise. Or water is also given to the beasts of burden, when the care of the flesh is arranged how it should be had, that it be not spent on pleasure and not denied from necessity; hence Romans 13: Make not provision for the flesh in its concupiscences; and Ephesians 5: No man ever hated his own flesh.
24.22: 24.22 The man took forth, etc. JEROME. A beka, which is here put for a didrachma, is half an ounce: a shekel, which in Latin, but corruptly, is called siclus, is an ounce. GREGORY. Because the preacher adorns the hearing of the Church by obedience, and the hands by work. The earrings are of two shekels, the bracelets ten, because the first virtue of obedience is in charity, which is the love of God and neighbor; and the good work is perfected by the fulfilling of the Decalogue, that when good things have begun to be done, no evil be done.
24.25: 24.25 And straw also. Because the Church, receiving spiritual things, renders to the preachers earthly stipends; hence 1 Corinthians 9: If we have sown unto you spiritual things, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things? A spacious place. From the former people the Church showed that she knew the law of nature, and received the preaching in the wide bosom of charity: for to the teacher a spacious dwelling is the breadth of charity in the heart of the hearer; hence 2 Corinthians 6: You are not straitened in us, but in your own bowels; as if: Enlarge the place of your mind for receiving doctrine, contract it for thinking carnal things.
24.29: 24.29 He had, etc. Because the carnal, joined to the faithful, while they behold the spiritual gifts, suspended in admiration, though not up to works, yet up to faith admit the preaching: for while they consider the good shining with miracles, they do not refuse what they hear of eternity, although, not following the Church in morals, they remain in carnal conduct. He had, however. Because there are carnal men joined to the faithful, by whose familiarity they sometimes come forth to hear the word, and seeing the gifts of God bestowed on the faithful they wonder, and perceive the word in the heart, which they do not strive to fulfill by good morals.
24.33: 24.33 I will not eat. Because there are those who are ready to keep teachers by temporal stipends: but those teachers refuse to receive them unless they first obtain eternal things. For if in souls they find no fruit, they scorn to take stipends for bodies; they do not wash their feet, because they relieve the desires of their labor with no consolation.
24.37: 24.37 And my master made me swear, etc. AUGUSTINE as above. The sense is the same, not all the words, either themselves or so said; which is to be said on account of those who slander the evangelists because they do not wholly agree in some words, when the matter and sense are the same; for one man wrote this book, who, what he said above when Abraham commanded, or the rest, could have put if he judged it pertinent to the matter: since the truth of the narration requires only that there be truth of things and meanings, by which the will for the sake of which the words are spoken is sufficiently apparent.
24.42: 24.42 I came therefore today, etc. JEROME. In the Hebrew it is written, etc., down to let the Jews therefore show somewhere almah placed where it sounds young woman and not virgin.
24.53: 24.53 And bringing forth, etc. GREGORY as above. After the servant obtained the cause of the marriage, etc., down to He gave them to Rebecca. Rebecca is not adorned with the gold of Bethuel, because the ornaments of the barbarous and unskilled are not worthy. She receives ornaments from the house of Abraham, because patience is adorned from the house of wisdom; from the servant of Abraham she receives earrings, that is, golden words in the ears; and bracelets, that is, golden works in the hands, and other ornaments; by which various kinds of virtues are figured.
24.59: 24.59 And her nurse. It was seemly that a virgin proceeding to a marriage without her parents should be cherished with the solace of a nurse.
24.61: 24.61 So Rebecca, etc. GREGORY. Because the Church has with her souls of lesser merit, which follow her in morals: but are not advanced to the couch of contemplation. She also had some young men in her company, because with the prophets there were those who lived well, though they had not the spirit of prophecy: and with the apostles and teachers, those who held their way of life and yet did not preach. Who in haste, etc. The servant returns in haste to his master, because preachers, when they obtain the life of their hearers, present it to God, from whose gift they have it, not to themselves.
24.62: 24.62 At that time Isaac, etc. GREGORY as above. The Lord is living and seeing, etc., down to now the crown of thorns, now the cross he bore. He dwelt, etc. PATERIUS on Genesis from the words of GREGORY. Isaac, when Rebecca came, dwelt in the south country, because Christ, when the Church came to him, abode in the minds of those whom not the cold of the body but the fervor of charity held: such were Anna, Simeon, and some of the people of the Jews.
24.63: 24.63 And he was gone forth, etc. JEROME. By the south country he signifies Gerar, whence he had been led to be sacrificed. He went out to meditate in the field. In the Hebrew it is read: Isaac went out to speak in the field, the evening being now inclined; where it is signified that the Lord alone prayed on the mountain, and Isaac, who was a type of the Lord, as a just man went out from the house to prayer at the ninth hour, or before sunset, and offered spiritual victims to God. GREGORY as above. The field is the world, into which Christ went forth, because he deigned to appear visibly. Hence Habakkuk 3: You went forth for the salvation of your people. Isaac went out to meditate in the field, because Christ, giving the form of humility, showed the exercise of longsuffering, the examples of passion and patience, as young men exercised in the use of arms are accustomed to meditate. The meditation of arms is the frequenting of the passion. For he who endured scourges, spitting, the lance and the cross allowed the passion even unto death to be frequented in himself. We call the passions arms, because by them we are freed from adversaries; hence Luke 21: In your patience you shall possess your souls. The evening being now inclined, etc. Because he took up the exercises of the passions near the end of the world; hence Psalm 140: The lifting up of my hands as evening sacrifice.
24.64: 24.64 She alighted from the camel, etc. GREGORY, Morals book 1, ch. 14. Rebecca is brought to Isaac on a camel, etc., down to carry riches on the winding backs of camels.
24.65: 24.65 Who is that man, etc. GREGORY in Paterius. Rebecca, seeing Isaac, learns who he is by inquiring of the servant: because the Church, by the words of the prophets and apostles, understands what she ought to believe of Christ. She soon covered herself with her cloak, because the more she penetrates the mysteries of Christ, the more she is confounded over her past life. Hence she endeavors to cover her weakness with her cloak; and she who before was borne freely on the camel, descending, is covered with shame, to whom it is said as if more modestly: What fruit had you then in those things of which you are now ashamed? But she, etc. JEROME. Another edition has teristrum, which even now is a kind of Arabian garment with which the women of that province are veiled.
24.67: 24.67 Who brought her in, etc. GREGORY as above. Isaac brought her into the tent of his mother and took her to wife, because in the place of the Synagogue, from which Christ was born, he loves the Church: that she who had been nearest by kinship, that is by predestination, may become a wife joined by love. And he loved her so much, etc. GREGORY as above. Because by the gain of the Church Christ wiped away the sorrow over the loss of the Synagogue, because while the Church coming from the Gentiles is led up to the couch of contemplation, Judea is held as nothing. Isaac also is called laughter, Rebecca patience: laughter from joy, patience from tribulation. And though the Church is now suspended in the contemplation of heavenly joy, she has in herself still something to grieve over from the weight of the flesh. Isaac and Rebecca are joined, that is laughter and patience, according to that Romans 12: Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation, that prosperity may gladden from contemplation, and adversity disturb from tribulation.
25.1: 25.1 And Abraham married another wife, etc. ISIDORE. Allegorically. Sarah being dead, Abraham took Keturah. Not through incontinence, since he was already advanced in years: nor for the procuring of children, because seed like the stars of heaven had been promised him from Isaac. But as Hagar and Ishmael figured the carnal of the Old Testament, so Keturah and her sons figure the heretics, who think they belong to the New Testament. But both are concubines, only Sarah is wife; hence Canticles 6: One is my dove, etc. Allegorically. After the assumption of the Church many souls deceived by heretical depravity adhered to Christ, who begot not Catholics but schismatics, who divided the unity of the Church: whom the sons of Keturah, who are numbered below, signify. JEROME, in Hebrew Questions. Keturah, in Hebrew, joined, etc., down to for the more one is weary in the flesh, the stronger he is in spirit and fit for the embraces of wisdom.
25.3: 25.3 The sons of Dedan were Asshurim, and Letushim, and Leummim. But of Midian were born Ephah and Epher and Hanoch and Abida. JEROME. They think Asshurim is translated into merchants, etc., down to and the regions of India occupied by many of the sons of Abraham by Keturah.
25.5: 25.5 And Abraham gave, etc. ISIDORE. Because gifts are given to the sons of concubines, that is of the carnal; but heretics or Jews do not come to the promised kingdom, because they follow carnal gains; Isaac alone is heir, because the children of the flesh are not reckoned in the seed, but the children of the promise.
25.8: 25.8 And decaying he died in a good old age, and of long life, and full of days, and was gathered to his people. And they buried him, etc. JEROME. It is wrongly added in the Septuagint: Abraham died decaying, because it is not fitting for Abraham to decay or be diminished. That also which we have put, in a good old age an old man and full, is put in the Greek codices more fully, full of days; which, though it seems to explain the sense, in that he departed full of light and the works of the day, yet makes more for the anagogical sense if full is put simply. The Greek gloss. Behold, Moses knew the life of the world to come, for no one can be added to those who are not.
25.12: 25.12 These are the generations, etc. These peoples are reckoned before the sons of Isaac, who, though they are of the seed of Abraham, are yet not reckoned in the seed, because first is that which is of the soul, then that which is spiritual. Hence after the reckoning of the carnal, the genealogy of Isaac is set down, of whom the promise was made, and the succession of the elect to be propagated.
25.13: 25.13 And these are the names of his sons in their names and generations. The firstborn of Ishmael Nebaioth, then Kedar, and Adbeel, etc. JEROME. Twelve sons are born to Ishmael, the firstborn Nebaioth, from whom the whole region from the Euphrates to the Red Sea is called Nabathea, which is part of Arabia. For their families' towns, villages and tribes are celebrated by their names. From one of these Kedar in the desert, and Dumah another region, and Tema to the south, and Kedemah, otherwise Chethma, toward the east, are named. What we read at the end of the chapter according to the Septuagint, he dwelt over against all his brethren, the truer is what we have put, he died before all his brethren, that is, he died in the hands of his sons, his children still surviving. For sons are called brethren; hence Jacob: Let it be set before my brethren, and your brethren, and let them judge between us. For it is not to be believed that Jacob, besides his own children, had any brethren with him.
25.16: 25.16 Twelve princes of their tribes. And the years of the life of Ishmael were made, etc. The number twelve, as it is hallowed in the apostles and apostolic men, so it is execrable in the reprobate against the faith of the Trinity and the Gospel spread through the four parts of the world.
25.18: 25.18 And he dwelt from Havilah as far as Shur, which looks toward Egypt, etc. The region which Pishon encircled, from Havilah, grandson of Noah, was so called, and it is a wilderness toward the face of Egypt. Shur also is a wilderness between Kadesh and Bered, extending the desert to the Red Sea and the borders of Egypt.
25.20: 25.20 From Mesopotamia, sister of Laban. A barren region, so called in Greek because it is in the middle between the two rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates. For middle in Greek is meso, and potamos is a river; hence hippopotamus, that is, the river horse.
25.21: 25.21 And he besought, but the children struggled together in her womb, etc. JEROME. The Septuagint put by pushing or collision, they were playing or kicking; Aquila, the sons contended in her womb. Symmachus, like a ship they were borne on the surface. GREGORY, Dialogues 1, 8. What the saints accomplish by praying, etc., down to for he in whom God had predestined to multiply the seed of Abraham obtained by prayer that he should have children. Who heard her. CHRYSOSTOM. Do not think that she obtained at once and immediately what she wished: for she remained twenty years praying and beseeching God. For as he taught us how many years he had when he took Rebecca, namely forty, so he assigned to us how old Isaac was when his sons were born. He was sixty, it says, when the little ones were born. And she went, etc. AUGUSTINE, Questions on Genesis, vol. 3. It is asked where she went, since there were not yet prophets or priests of the tabernacle or temple of the Lord. Perhaps to the place where Abraham set up the altar. But how the answers were given there Scripture is silent; or by some priest? it would be strange, if there was one, that he was not named and no mention made of priests. Perhaps there, when by praying they had laid their desires before him, they slept, that they might be warned in sleep: or Melchizedek was still living, whose excellence was so great that it was doubted whether he was man or angel. Or perhaps even at that time there were men of God in whom God could be inquired of. Whichever of these it was, or perhaps something else. Yet Rebecca, according to Scripture, inquired of the Lord, and deserved his answer.
25.23: 25.23 Who answering said: Two nations, etc. AUGUSTINE. By historical propriety the answer is found fulfilled, when, for the sake of Israel, that is Jacob, the younger son overcame the Idumeans, that is the nation which Esau propagated, and made them tributaries through David; which they long were until King Joram, 4 Kings 8. For then the Idumeans rebelled and shook the yoke from their neck, as Isaac prophesied when he blessed the younger instead of the elder, and said the same to the elder when he afterwards blessed him.
25.24: 25.24 Now the time, etc. JEROME. Where we have put hairy, the Hebrew has seyr; hence Esau, as we read elsewhere, was called seyr, that is hairy. Immediately the other, etc. ISIDORE. This done figuratively is known even to the unbelieving Jews: how the people of the Church overcame the people of the Synagogue, and the people of the Jews, elder in time, served the younger people of the Christians. BEDE on this chapter, vol. 2. In each one this can also be said. Two nations and two peoples are within us, namely of vices and of virtues; the one younger, the other elder: for the evil are more than the good, and vices more than virtues. Yet the people overcomes the people, and the elder shall serve the younger, namely the flesh the spirit, and vices virtues. Esau goes first, red, and all like a hairy skin: then Jacob comes out holding his brother's heel; for the former people, defiled with the blood of the prophets and of Christ, surrounded by the filth of sin and wickedness: whose heel the younger held, because the younger people overcame the elder.
25.27: 25.27 Esau became, etc. GREGORY. He signifies the life of those who, poured out in external pleasures, follow the flesh. He is also called a husbandman, because lovers of the world cultivate the exterior things as much as they leave their interior uncultivated. Plain. GREGORY. Because the simple shun being scattered by external cares, they abide in thought and in the dwelling of conscience. For he dwells in tents who confines himself within the secrets of the mind, lest while he gapes after many things outside he withdraw alienated from himself in thought.
25.29: 25.29 And Jacob boiled, etc. JEROME. Red or ruddy: in Hebrew it is called Edom: from this, that Esau sold his birthright for red food, he received the name of ruddy, that is, Edom.
25.31: 25.31 To whom Jacob said, etc. ISIDORE. That Esau sold his birthright to his younger brother for food, and afterwards was deprived of the promised paternal blessing, signifies the Jewish people: who in Exodus is called the firstborn son of God, and for the gains of the world not only lost the honor of its primacy but did not deserve to obtain the reward of the heavenly kingdom prepared. Hence by way of reproach it is said, Matthew 12: The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to the Gentiles, etc. The birthright, however, was a priestly garment, in which the elder sons, clothed, with the blessing of the father offered victims to God as pontiffs: of this gift, by the desire of earthly love, the Jews were deprived, together with the glory of the future kingdom.
25.33: 25.33 Esau swore, etc. GREGORY, Morals book 30, ch. 13. It is to be known that the vice of gluttony tempts us in five ways, etc., down to and not what the lust of eating suggests.
26.1: 26.1 And a famine arising in the land, etc. AUGUSTINE, Questions on Genesis, vol. 3. It is asked when it was that Isaac went to Gerar, etc., down to that we may understand that temporal things can neither be given nor ought to prosper except from the one God.
26.8: 26.8 And when they had passed, etc. ISIDORE. From the time of Christ to the times of Constantine the faith was preached not in the assembly of peoples but as through hiding places, the Christians gathered in secret: at length the Christian princes of the age, seeing through the miracles of Christ his majesty tempered to human weakness, that they might be associated and be two in one flesh, now permitted the sacrament of Christ and the Church to be preached openly, and grieved that it had been long hidden. He saw him playing, etc. AUGUSTINE. What it means in the sacrament of Christ and the Church, etc., down to that he might dwell in us.
26.12: 26.12 And Isaac sowed in that land, etc. JEROME. Although Isaac sowed in a strange land, I do not think he had so great a fertility of barley. Hence I think better what is had in the Hebrew, and what Aquila translated: He found in that year a hundredfold by estimation. Scripture, silent on the kind of fruits which he multiplied a hundredfold, seems to have shown in him the multiplication of all virtues.
26.14: 26.14 Therefore envying, etc. ISIDORE. Isaac, Christ, who first wishes to dig wells, etc., down to we shall go. And they stopped the wells, etc. GREGORY. Morally. Often when we attend to the divine words, we bear more heavily the snares of the demons; they sprinkle the dust of earthly thoughts on our mind to darken the eyes of intention from the light of inward vision. For we dig wells when we penetrate the depths of Scripture, which the Philistines secretly fill: because they bring in earthly thoughts and take away the water of divine knowledge, hence Psalm 118: Depart from me, you malignant, and I will search the commandments of my God.
26.17: 26.17 And he departing, etc. JEROME. And Isaac went from thence, and came to the valley of Gerar, and dwelt there. For valley they have torrent in the Hebrew. For Isaac, after he became great, could never dwell in a valley, but in a torrent. Of which it is written, Psalm 109: He shall drink of the torrent in the way. Of which Elijah drank in the time of famine; but because he was not perfect as Christ, the torrent dried up for him. But Christ was delivered even in the torrent, dedicating our regeneration and the sacrament of baptism.
26.18: 26.18 He digged other wells, etc. ISIDORE from Gregory. Isaac digs wells among a foreign nation: in which we are admonished in this pilgrimage to penetrate the depths of thoughts, and until the water of true understanding returns, that the hand of inquiry grow not slack in drawing out the earthly things of the heart. The Philistines lying in wait fill the wells, because unclean spirits, when they see us diligently digging, bring in the troubles of temptations to our thoughts.
26.20: 26.20 Against the shepherds, etc. JEROME. Aquila and Symmachus translated adverse and contrary, but in the Hebrew it is Satan; whence it is plain that Satan is interpreted the adversary.
26.22: 26.22 Largeness. In Hebrew Rehoboth, broad places. Hence is proved what was said above, chapter X: He built Nineveh and Rehoboth, that is, its streets. Now he has enlarged, etc. Isaac is enlarged, and filled the whole earth with the knowledge of the Trinity: and throughout the whole world set the breadth of the Church, first known in Judea, and named in Israel: afterwards their sound went out into all the earth, Psalm 18, that is of the apostles, who through the whole world dug wells, and showed water to all, baptizing all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, Matthew 18. The wells of Abraham, which he opened, he called as his father had: for Moses and the prophets are called among us by their own names, and the names of these wells are not changed.
26.26: 26.26 To which place, etc. JEROME. Abimelech does not always have peace with Isaac, etc., down to and there are many other things in which the philosophers differ or agree with us. For Ahuzzath, the best man, the Hebrew has the company of his friends, so that it signifies both a man and the crowd of friends who had come with the king: among whom was Phicol, the chief of that army. Abimelech and Ahuzzath, etc. ISIDORE on Genesis, vol. 5. Two came with Abimelech: Ahuzzath, his son-in-law, etc., down to he is a debtor to the wise and the foolish.
26.32: 26.32 And behold they came. JEROME. I do not know how it is in the Septuagint: and the servants of Isaac came telling him of the well which they had dug, and said to him: We have not found water. And he called its name Oath. For what etymology is it, that it should therefore be called Oath, etc., down to it does not fit that Isaac should not find water.
27.1: 27.1 And Isaac was old, etc. HIPPOLYTUS martyr, from Jerome, letter to Damasus, vol. 1. Mystically. Isaac bears the image of God the Father, Rebecca of the Holy Spirit, Esau of the former people and of the devil, Jacob of the Church and Christ. The old age of Isaac signifies the consummation of the world; the dim eyes, that faith has perished from the world, and the light of religion been neglected. Because the elder son is called, it is the reception of the law of the Jews. Because the father loved his food and his hunting: they are men saved from error, whom each just man hunts by his teaching. The word of God, the blessing of the promise, and the hope of the future kingdom, in which they are to reign with Christ and to keep the true sabbath. Rebecca full of the Holy Spirit, knowing what she had heard before she bore, that the elder shall serve the younger: she bears the form of the Holy Spirit, who, what she knew would be in Christ, meditated beforehand in Jacob, speaks to the younger son. Go to the flock and bring me two best kids; prefiguring the fleshly coming of the Savior, in which he would free those who were held liable to sins. For kids everywhere signify sinners. Two are commanded to be brought, that the assumption of two peoples may be signified. Tender, namely, and human, teachable, namely, and of an innocent soul. The robe of Esau is the faith, that is, the Scriptures of the Hebrews, which were given first to them, with which the people of the Gentiles was afterwards clothed; the skins put about his arms are the sins of both peoples, which Christ in the stretching out of his hands fastened with himself to the cross: for he in his body bore not his own, but others' sins.
27.2: 27.2 And he called Esau. ISIDORE on Genesis, vol. 5. Esau a hunter, and a husbandman, Jacob a plain man dwelling in tents. Esau signifies the Hebrew people, Jacob the Gentile people. Isaac signifies God, who made both peoples sons to himself, that one by the law, this by faith. Esau was a husbandman, because the Jew served God for earthly things, to whom it was not said that he should be poor in spirit, meek, peaceable, merciful, suffering persecution, that he might have a plentiful reward in heaven; but: If you keep my commandments, I will give you rains in their seasons, etc., which pertain to the delights of the flesh. He was also a hunter, because by the shedding of the blood of rams and calves and goats he appeased God. Jacob, a plain man, dwelt in tents, because the elect from the Gentiles by faith and will strove to please God. By tents we understand the various churches throughout the world or the various orders.
27.3: 27.3 Take your arms, etc. Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his hunting. Rebecca loved Jacob; Isaac figures God, Rebecca the foreknowledge of God, because God loved the people of the Jews inasmuch as he was constantly appeased by their offerings. But foreseeing that the people of the Gentiles would be much better, by the grace of his foreknowledge he loved it the more. Esau lingering at the hunt, to bring his father food from wild animals and be blessed, the mother applied Jacob to receive the blessing from his father: because the Jews still linger in legal things and are slow to come to the faith of Christ, the mother, grace, offered the Gentiles, eagerly receiving the faith, to receive the blessing owed to the Jews. How they deserved the gift of the blessing, the works of Jacob testify, which he did to receive the blessing.
27.6: 27.6 She said to her son Jacob: I heard your father speaking, etc. Allegorically. By the two kids we can understand the confession of sins of the Gentile people and penance. The kids are the best, because confession of sins and penance is very acceptable to God. Hence Luke 15: There shall be joy in heaven upon one sinner that does penance, etc. Historically. By one sinner he understands the Gentile people, by the ninety-nine just the Jews, who seemed to themselves just in the observance of the law. Hence Luke 16: You are they who justify yourselves before men, etc.; who are put in an imperfect number, because the law brought no one to perfection.
27.14: 27.14 She prepared the meats, etc. ISIDORE. Mystically. By the delicious dishes which are prepared from the kids for Isaac, we understand the works of penance, etc., down to he often brings past sins before the eyes of the mind.
27.15: 27.15 And with the garments of Esau, etc. JEROME. In this place the Hebrews hand down that the firstborn performed the office of priests, and had a priestly vestment, in which clothed they offered victims, before Aaron was chosen to the priesthood.
27.20: 27.20 How, he said, could you find it so quickly, my son? HIPPOLYTUS. Isaac asks Jacob why he came so quickly, marveling, namely, at the swift faith of believers. Delicious meats are offered, because the victim pleasing to God is the salvation of sinners. Because after the eating the blessing follows, and he enjoys its scent, he openly proclaims the power of the resurrection and the kingdom. Behold the smell of my son is as the smell of a full field. This is the blessing. With the odor of the name of Christ, as with a field, the world is filled. The blessing is of the dew of heaven, that is the rain of the divine word; and of the fatness of the earth, that is the gathering of peoples; plenty of corn and wine, this is the multitude which he gathers from the sacrament of his body and blood. Peoples serve him, that is, the converted Gentiles. Tribes adore him, believers converted through circumcision. He is lord of his brethren, that is, of the Jews. The sons of his mother adore him, because according to the flesh he was born of her: whoever curses him shall be cursed; and he that blesses him shall be blessed. Christ is blessed from the mouth of a people ignorant of the Father, that is, truly spoken of, but by the Jews another is thought blessed, who is awaited by the erring.
27.25: 27.25 Which when he had eaten, being offered, etc. Mystically. After Isaac took the food, Jacob offered him wine: so by the food the works of the active life are designated; by the wine, which alienates minds, the contemplative life is understood, which makes the minds of the elect alienated from love of the world. After food and drink. Jacob is blessed, because they receive the heavenly blessing from God who strive to please him by good works to the end.
27.27: 27.27 Blessing him, he said, etc. GREGORY, hom. 6 on Ezekiel. The one is sent to hunt, etc., down to which the elder going outside left within. GREGORY, ibid. Isaac, his eyes growing dim, blessed his son Jacob without knowing him; he foresaw what was to come, and did not know who stood present. For it is agreed that the Jews, who learned the law fully, knew the coming of Christ. Hence Matthew 2, Herod inquires of the chief priests where Christ should be born; and they at once answered, In Bethlehem. They knew therefore before him whom, at the time of the passion, when they despised him, they did not know; their former knowledge and later ignorance is signified by Isaac growing dim; who, while he blessed Jacob, foresaw what would befall him in the future, but did not know who stood present. So the people of the Jews received the mysteries of prophecy, but kept blind eyes in contemplation, because they did not see the present one of whom they foresaw many things in the future. For they could not discern him placed before them whose coming in power they had announced long before. GREGORY, hom. 10 on Ezekiel, vol. 2. Isaac does not know the son whom he blessed, etc., down to and because through some it rises to contemplation, through others it grows fat in the works of the active life. It follows:
27.28: 27.28 May God give you of the dew of heaven, etc. The dew falls from above and subtly, and we receive of the dew of heaven as often as through the infusion of inward contemplation we see something faintly of the things above. But when we do good works through the body, we are enriched with the fatness of the earth. Abundance of corn, etc. ISIDORE. This is the multitude which he gathers from the sacrament of his body and blood.
27.30: 27.30 Esau came, etc. Esau returns late to his father, because the former people will be converted at the end. Hence Psalm 58: They shall return at evening, and shall suffer hunger like dogs, and shall go round about the city. And elsewhere: They opened their mouths as one eating in secret.
27.33: 27.33 Isaac was struck with fear. The elder son asking again for the promised blessing, Isaac was struck with fear, and recognized that he had blessed one for another; nor is he indignant, the sacrament being known, but confirmed the blessing, saying: And I have blessed him, and he shall be blessed. This is the first blessing of Isaac given to the younger people of the Christians. But the elder son is not wholly despised, because when the fullness of the Gentiles shall have come in, then all Israel shall be saved. Of this second blessing there is a prophecy. In the fatness of the earth, and in the dew of heaven from above shall your blessing be. In the fatness of the earth, that is, in the fruitfulness of things and the power of the kingdom which was in that people; and in the dew of heaven, in the words of God. For to them were committed the words of God, and the covenants of the law. You shall live by the sword: because that people, given to blood, exercised slaughter on Christ and the prophets. And you shall serve your younger brother, that is, the Christian people. And the time shall come when you shall shake off and loose his yoke from your neck; when namely, converted by the knowledge of faith and the grace of Christ, you shall lay down the burden of the law; when then you shall no longer serve the younger, but by faith shall be called brother. Isaac was struck with fear, etc. That a certain alienation of mind might follow, which is called ecstasy, as is wont to happen in revelations of great things. Hence it is to be understood that Isaac was spiritually admonished to confirm the blessing on Jacob, with whom he ought rather to have been angry, because he deceived his father. In Adam also ecstasy preceded, before he said: They shall be two in one flesh, Genesis 2, which is a great sacrament in Christ and in the Church. And I have blessed him, etc. ALCUIN. If the will of a just man is good, why is it that Isaac blessed not Esau whom he wished but Jacob whom he did not wish? The will of a just man, as far as conscience, is good: but God alone judges of the future. Isaac in the human way thought the elder son should be blessed: but God, who knows hidden things, showed the younger worthy of blessing, to show that the blessing is not of man but of God: therefore in Numbers it is said to Moses and Aaron the priests: Put my name upon the children of Israel. I the Lord will bless them, Numbers 6. It is for the priest to bless, to bestow the effect of God. When Isaac understood by the spirit of prophecy that the blessing was destined for the younger, he said, I have blessed, and he shall be blessed.
27.36: 27.36 Rightly is his name called Jacob: for he hath supplanted me, etc. JEROME. Jacob is interpreted supplanter. From this therefore, that he first deceived his brother, he alludes to the name, who was therefore first called Jacob because at birth he caught his brother's heel.
27.40: 27.40 And you shall serve your brother, etc. Because the Idumeans were tributaries of Israel, who is called Jacob. And the time shall come when you shall shake off and loose his yoke. , etc. This was fulfilled when the Idumeans rebelled that they might not be under Judah. And the time shall come, etc. As if: The Jewish people will be freed from the servitude of sin at the end, that when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, all Israel may be saved, Romans 11.
27.41: 27.41 And he said in his heart. Since Scripture says that Esau in his heart thought of his brother's death, how or by whom were these things told to Rebecca? But it is given to be understood that all things were revealed to her by God. On account of the incurable hatred of the Jews, by the spirit of counsel it was commanded to the apostles that, leaving Judea, they should pass to the Gentiles. The days of mourning shall come, etc. For he did not wish to do this while his father lived, lest he incur his hatred and be cursed by him. DIODORUS. What is written, Esau said in his heart, signifies that Esau wished his brother's death not by sudden anger but with the full consent of his mind.
27.42: 27.42 These things were told to Rebecca, etc. Here the mother's counter-move is consequently set down, when it is said, These things were told. From which it is plain that Esau did not so hide the aforesaid plot in his heart that it did not appear outwardly in signs and words. Sending and calling Jacob, etc. To induce him to give place to wrath and withdraw for a time. It follows: Why shall I be deprived of both my sons? etc. As if she said: If he assail you, it may be that you will both be killed; or if one remains, he must be a fugitive from me. And Rebecca said, etc. Because Jacob could not fittingly depart without his father's knowledge, Rebecca turned to inducing Isaac to send his son Jacob to Laban, to take a wife there, saying: I am weary, etc. That is on account of the wives of Esau: but she did not tell Isaac the other cause, namely the plot of Esau for the death of Jacob, lest in his old age he be too much afflicted. If Jacob take a wife, etc. As if she said: If you love my life, send him to the house of my brother, that there he may take a wife.
28.1: 28.1 Isaac therefore called, etc. AUGUSTINE, Questions on Genesis. What the Latin codices have: Go into Mesopotamia to the house of Bethuel, etc., the Greek have: Flee into Mesopotamia, etc., so that it may be understood that Isaac also understood that Esau had thought of his brother's death. And he set out. ISIDORE. Jacob, fleeing the wiles of his brother, leaving his father's house and parents, goes into a far country to take a wife. Similarly Christ, leaving his parents according to the flesh, that is the Jews, and his country, that is Jerusalem, and all the regions of Judea, went to the Gentiles to receive the Church for himself, according to that of Hosea 2: I will call that which was not my people, etc.
28.10: 28.10 So Jacob going out, etc. GREGORY, Morals book V, ch. 11, vol. 1. To sleep on the road, etc., down to for the Lord is sweet.
28.11: 28.11 He took of the stones, etc. ISIDORE. The sleep of Jacob on the road is the death of Christ on the cross. The stone put under his head is Christ according to his humanity, whom Jacob anointed, that Christ might be signified, for Christ in Greek is anointed in Latin. The head, however, is Christ as God. The stone therefore put under Jacob's head signifies the humanity of Christ joined to the God who assumes it. For the head of the man is Christ, the head of Christ is God, 1 Corinthians 11.
28.12: 28.12 And he saw in his sleep, etc. GREGORY, Register book 1, letter 24. Jacob signifies preachers, who not only seek the head of the Church, that is Christ, by contemplating, but descend to his members by compassion: which the angels ascending and descending show. Hence Moses frequently enters and goes out of the tabernacle; and he who within is rapt to contemplation is pressed without by the business of the infirm; within he considers secrets, without he bears the burdens of the carnal. He who in doubtful matters always ran back to the tabernacle consults the Lord before the ark of the testament, giving an example to rulers that when abroad they are in doubt what to arrange, they return to the mind as to the tabernacle, and as before the ark of the testament consult the Lord, seeking within themselves the pages of sacred speech about the matters they doubt. Morally. To sleep on the road is to rest in the way of this world from the hindrance of secular actions. Jacob sleeping saw angels: because they behold divine things who close their eyes to the appetite of temporal things: whose eyes, well closed, the devil opened, saying: In what day soever you shall eat thereof, your eyes shall be opened, Genesis 3. He saw in his sleep, etc. ISIDORE. The angels ascending and descending by the ladder are the evangelists and preachers of Christ, ascending to understand the Divinity; passing beyond all creation, that they may find in the beginning the Word with God, by whom all things were made. Descending, that they may find him made of a woman, made under the law, etc. In that ladder also from earth to heaven, from flesh to spirit: because in it the carnal, by advancing, as if ascending, become spiritual. To feed whom with milk the spiritual descend, because they cannot speak to them as to spiritual but as to carnal. He is above in the head, he below in his body, that is the Church; he is the ladder, who says, John 14: I am the way, etc. To him one ascends, that he may be understood in the heights: and one descends, that he may be nourished in the little members; through him they raise themselves, that they may await the sublime: and humble themselves, that they may announce him sublimely and temperately.
28.13: 28.13 I am the Lord God of Abraham, etc. Mystically it designates the command of the Divinity directed to the humanity of Christ, to whom the land, that is the Church, is promised; and to his seed, that is the Christian people. Hence Psalm 2: Ask of me, and I will give you the Gentiles for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession.
28.16: 28.16 And when he awoke, etc. Whoever, after the torpor of idleness, shall awake and by the exercise of good work truly rise up, will understand in the Church the surpassing grace of God and the entrance of the heavenly kingdom.
28.18: 28.18 Rising therefore, etc. AUGUSTINE, Questions on Genesis, vol. 3. That Jacob set up the stone he had put under his head as a pillar and poured oil upon it did nothing like idolatry: because neither then nor afterwards did he frequent the stone by adoring it or sacrificing to it; but it was a sign and a prophecy pertaining to the anointing, whence Christ is named.
28.19: 28.19 And he called the name of the city Bethel, etc. JEROME, on Hebrew places. From what was said, How terrible is this place, etc., he gives the place the name Bethel, that is house of God, which before was called Luz, that is nut or almond. Hence some ridiculously think the Hebrew word ulam is the name of a city, when ulam is interpreted formerly. The order of the reading is therefore this: He called the name of that place Bethel, and formerly Luz was the name of the city. The ancient writings, however, are full of the word ulam or olam, which means nothing but formerly or before the porch, or lintel, or doorposts, etc.
28.22: 28.22 And this stone shall be called the house of God, etc. It is a prophecy of the house of God to be there, where also he himself, returning, sacrificed to God.
29.1: 29.1 Then Jacob setting out, etc. He saw a well in the field, etc. The water of the well is the knowledge of the Old Testament: which a stone closed, because the letter of the law hid the spiritual sense in it; but when Christ came the stone was removed, when by the preaching of the New Testament the shadow of the law was shut out and the truth of the Gospel laid open. Allegorically. By the well baptism, by the field the world is expressed: by the three flocks lying by the well are signified those who pertain to taking up the faith of the Trinity, humbly seeking the grace of baptism. The stone is the hardness of unbelief, which being cast away, the baptism of life is received. The shepherds are the prelates of the Church, who, the stone being removed, desire through Jacob to water the flocks: because Christ taking away unbelief from the hearts of those whom he predestined to the sacrament of baptism, they are washed by the wave of purification.
29.11: 29.11 And he kissed her. AUGUSTINE. It was a custom, especially in that simplicity of the ancients, for kinsmen to kiss kinsmen, and today it is done in many places. But it may be asked how she received a kiss from a stranger, if Jacob only afterwards told his kinship? It is to be understood therefore: either that he, who knew the kinship, rushed confidently to the kiss, or that Scripture afterwards narrated it by recapitulation, since Jacob first told who he was.
29.16: 29.16 The name of the elder was Leah, etc. Victorinus the martyr interpreted Rachel and Leah as a likeness of the Church and the Synagogue. He thinks Leah, the elder, signifies the Synagogue, because she first begot the people of God: who is said to be blear-eyed because the law given through Moses was veiled and sealed. Rachel the younger and beautiful, first barren, afterwards fruitful, signifies the Church, which is later in time, but holy in body and spirit. Her eyes are comely, because they deserved to see the Gospel. But long barren while the Synagogue bore the people. For Rachel Jacob served, and Leah is substituted for her: because Christ, to take the Church to himself, first joined the Synagogue to himself.
29.20: 29.20 So Jacob served seven years for Rachel. The servitude of Jacob of seven years for two wives signifies the time of the present life, which revolves in seven days; in which the Lord took the form of a servant, obedient to the Father unto death. Jacob served, because the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, Matthew 20: He fed sheep, and Christ said, John 10: I am the good shepherd. He took for his wages the spotted flock: Christ gathered to himself the variety of diverse nations. He placed three rods with the bark stripped in the troughs of water, that by looking at them the sheep might multiply: and our Lord in the water of baptism set before the faithful people the names of the three Persons, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, that he who has looked upon this with full heart may become a sheep of God. And they seemed to him but a few days, etc. How is this said, to be inquired, when even a short time seems long to lovers? It is said therefore because of the labor of the service, which love made easy. AUGUSTINE, book XXII against Faustus. Four wives are charged against Jacob as a huge crime. But since it was then the custom, it was no crime; now it is a crime because it is not the custom, etc., down to except the burning of carnal concupiscence. ISIDORE, on Genesis, vol. 5. Jacob's two wives are free, for both are daughters of the remission of sins, etc., down to and saw in the beginning the Word with God, and wishes to bring forth and cannot, because who shall declare his generation? Acts 8. ISIDORE. Jacob's two free wives, because two lives are preached to us in the body of Jesus Christ, etc., down to But this cannot be on the earth of the dying, which is signified by these words.
29.26: 29.26 It is not the custom in our place, etc. THE SAME, ibid. The elder is that which is earlier in time, etc., down to so one must aim at one, but for this much must be borne. THE SAME, ibid. Accordingly the life that befits the study of contemplation, etc., down to hence below 30: Rachel envied her sister. THE SAME, ibid. Accordingly because pure understanding of that divine substance, etc., down to not because divinity.
30.14: 30.14 And Reuben going out, etc. AUGUSTINE, book XXII against Faustus. Why Scripture did not pass over the deed, etc., down to and whatever is piously and wisely said of this may be wholesomely taken, in whole or in part, without the phantasm of carnal thought. And Reuben going out, etc. AUGUSTINE. Historically. I know that some suppose of this kind that, taken as food by barren women, it produces fertility, and so Rachel pressed to have it, which I do not think, nor would she have conceived thus then. But now that the Lord gave Leah offspring after two others, from that night's labors, there is nothing for us to suspect from the mandrake of such a thing as we have experienced in no woman. For when I myself saw these apples, and congratulated myself that this place of sacred reading had befallen me, for it is a rare thing, I examined their nature as far as I could, not by any science remote from common sense, which teaches the virtues of roots and powers of herbs, but as far as sight, smell and taste report, I found the thing beautiful, sweet-smelling, but insipid in taste. Why therefore the woman so greatly desired it I do not know, unless perhaps for the rarity of the fruit and the pleasantness of its smell.
30.32: 30.32 Go round all your flocks, etc. JEROME, in Hebrew Questions. The sense is much confused in the Septuagint, etc., down to the end is near. ALCUIN. Why Jacob is not accused of fraud in this place: he did this without doubt as a prophet, nor is it to be believed that he did it without spiritual revelation.
31.1: 31.1 But after he heard, etc. He changed my wages, etc. JEROME in Hebrew Questions. For what we have put, he changed my wages ten times, the Septuagint put ten years: though the Hebrew word monim sounds a number rather than years; and from what follows this sense is proved, that at every lambing he changed the condition upon Laban. If he saw spotted cattle born, he said: I want those born to me in future to be spotted; then Jacob did not put the rods in the channels, that the offspring might be of one color: which done, Laban said those cattle must be his share; so up to ten times the condition was changed: and whatever Laban had proposed should be born for him was turned to the opposite color. Now in six years ten breedings might seem incredible; but read Virgil, in whom it is said: Twice with young the flocks. The nature of Italian sheep and of Mesopotamia is said to be the same.
31.12: 31.12 For I have seen all, etc. From this we learn that Jacob did it with no evil guile, but by divine disposition, or because all things were done in figure. Hence he deserved to be comforted by an angelic vision.
31.13: 31.13 Now therefore arise. GREGORY, Morals 30, 16. After long servitude the Lord commanded Jacob to return to his country: then, without his father-in-law's knowledge, with his wives and company he hastened. Laban, however, overtook him in Mount Gilead, seeking his idols with fury, and did not find them. Laban in this place bears the type of the devil. For he is interpreted whitening. The devil, though full of darkness, transforms himself into an angel of light. Jacob served him, that is the Jewish people, from the part of the reprobate, of whom Christ was born according to the flesh.
31.32: 31.32 He knew not that Rachel had stolen the idols. JEROME. Where we read idols, in the Hebrew is written teraphim; which Aquila interprets figures or images. I say this that we may know what teraphim sounds like in the book of Judges. Against Mount Gilead, etc. Not that at that time the mountain was called Gilead, but by anticipation it is called by the name by which it was afterwards named. Who, taking his brethren, pursued, etc. GREGORY. Historically. By Laban the world can be expressed: which follows Jacob with fury, because it strives to oppress the elect, who are members of Christ. Jacob took away the daughter of the world or of the devil, when Christ joined the Church from the Gentiles to himself, to whom it is said through the prophet, Psalm 44: Forget your people, etc. In the idols avarice is signified, which is the service of idols. Laban coming did not find the idol at Jacob's, because, the riches of the world having been shown to our Redeemer, the devil found no trace of concupiscence. But what Jacob had not, Rachel covered by sitting, which is interpreted sheep, and signifies the Church. To sit is to seek the humility of penance. Hence Psalm 126: Rise up after you have sat. Rachel covers the idols by sitting, because the Church following Christ has covered the vice of earthly concupiscence by the humility of penance. Hence Psalm 13: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Rachel therefore signifies us who press down idols by sitting, if by penance we condemn the faults of avarice; which filth of avarice does not manfully hinder those running, but those walking effeminately are loosened by the blandishments of the world, which is signified by these words: According to the custom of women it has befallen me. For he made known that he suffered womanish things. That I might kiss my sons and daughters. In the manner of Scripture he calls his sons and daughters Jacob's, which calls kinsmen sons or brethren; hence in what follows: And Jacob said to his brethren: Bring stones. In the Gospel too the sons of Mary, the Lord's aunt, are called his brethren, Matthew 12. I feared lest you would violently take away your daughters, and whereas you accuse me of theft, etc. As if to say: therefore I did not make it known to you, lest by the bitterness of pursuit you overcome weak souls newly snatched from you.
31.40: 31.40 Day and night I was parched with heat and frost. Sleep fled from my eyes. Heat and cold had one effect.
31.46: 31.46 Bring stones, etc. JEROME, on Hebrew places. A heap in the Hebrew language, etc., down to in the speech in which he lived he had changed. ISIDORE. Mystically. Between believers, both Jews and Gentiles, the witness is the eminent stone in the likeness of Christ; and the heap of stones, which is the multitude of believers.
31.53: 31.53 Jacob swore, etc. By the fear, namely, with which he feared God, which he commended above, saying, And the fear, etc.
31.55: 31.55 And Laban by night, etc. Because Laban and Jacob went across the river, it can signify the two peoples coming to the Church through baptism. But Jacob going on beyond, Laban returned, because, the children of light advancing in virtues after baptism, the reprobate return to apostasy after Satan from the dignity received.
32.2: 32.2 These are the camps of God. Where the camps were placed, in the Hebrew is mahanaim; that we may know, if ever, interpreted, it is put in another place, what place it signifies. And beautifully, about to go to his enemy brother, he is received by choirs of angels accompanying him.
32.7: 32.7 Jacob feared, etc. AUGUSTINE, Questions on Genesis. It may be asked how he had faith in God's promises, that he said this. But it could be that Esau would overthrow his camp, and then after that affliction God would be present and fulfill what he promised. And we are admonished by this example that though we believe in God, we should yet do what is to be done for the safeguard of salvation. The words of Jacob also are to be considered, saying: God of my father Abraham, etc., because in these words both human weakness and the faith of piety appear.
32.10: 32.10 I passed over the Jordan, etc. By baptism the wall of the Gentiles is joined to that of the Jews: yet the fear of the Jews, which Esau signifies, is not lacking in the primitive Church.
32.11: 32.11 Deliver me from the hand, etc. He so prays that he tempers hope with fear and consoles fear with hope, signifying that we should take counsel for our life and our household, and yet invoke the help of God.
32.20: 32.20 I will appease him, etc. These things are interposed by the writer. For it is not the part of a prudent man to disclose his art, and so make himself suspected to those with whom he deals. GREGORY, hom. 14 on the Gospels, vol. 2. Mystically. Jacob, when he returns to his own parents, etc., down to that by inmost sweetness we may lay hold of God. And behold a man, etc. ISIDORE on Genesis, vol. 5. In this chiefly the image of the Lord's sacrament is figured, etc., down to that he may not beget any more.
32.28: 32.28 By no means, said Jacob, shall your name be called, but, etc. JEROME in Hebrew Questions. Josephus in the first book of Antiquities, etc., down to we are led rather by the authority of Scripture, and of the angel, or of God, who called him Israel, than by any secular eloquence.
32.30: 32.30 And Jacob called, etc. That also which follows, and he blessed him, and Jacob called the name of that place Peniel, saying, etc. In the Hebrew it is said Peniel, that we may know it to be the very place which in the other volumes of Scripture, according to the Hebrews, is read Penuel. GREGORY, Morals book IV, ch. 6. It is asked, since the Truth says: No man shall see my face; and: No man hath seen God at any time, how Jacob testifies: I have seen the Lord face to face? For human minds, the inner eye being purified, etc., down to hence 1 Corinthians 13: Then shall I know even as I am known.
33.1: 33.1 And Jacob lifting up his eyes divided the children of Leah and Rachel, etc. Aquila halved them, that he might make one wedge of the handmaids with their little ones, and another of the free women with their sons; and send the handmaids first, the free women second: he himself before all would run to meet his brother to adore him.
33.10: 33.10 For I have so seen, etc. AUGUSTINE, Questions on Genesis, vol. 3. Whether the words of a fearful and disturbed mind, etc., down to who are accustomed to hear and understand Greek.
33.14: 33.14 And I will follow, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked whether he promised his brother a lie. For this, as Scripture narrates, he did not do; but went on by the road that led to his own. Or perhaps he promised with a truthful mind, but afterwards, thinking otherwise, chose another course? Succoth. JEROME. Where we have tents, in the Hebrew is read Succoth. There is to this day a city beyond the Jordan with this name, in the region of Scythopolis, of which we wrote in the book of Places.
33.18: 33.18 And he passed over to Salem, etc. JEROME. A question arises how the city of Shechem is called Salem, when Jerusalem, in which Melchizedek reigned, was before called Salem. Either then both cities have one name, which we find of many places in Judea, that the same name of a city and place is in one tribe and another. Or we shall say that this Salem, which is now named for Shechem, is interpreted completed and perfect: and that which was afterwards called Jerusalem, peaceful. The word sounds both with the accent a little changed. The Hebrews hand down that the thigh of the limping Jacob was healed there: and therefore the city got the name of the healed and perfected.
34.1: 34.1 And Dinah went out, etc. GREGORY in Pastoral, ch. 30. Dinah goes out to see the women of a foreign region, when the mind, neglecting its own pursuits, caring for the actions of others, wanders outside its own order. Shechem, prince of the land, oppresses her, because the devil corrupts the one found in external cares. And his soul was glued to her, because he regards her as united to himself through iniquity. And because the mind, returning to itself from guilt, is affected and strives to weep over what was committed, the corrupter calls up before the eyes empty hope and security, so as to take away the usefulness of sadness. Hence it is added: And he comforted the sad one with soothing words. Now he says that others' deeds are graver; now that what was done is nothing; now he speaks of a merciful God and promises time for penance: so that while the mind is led by these things deceived, penance is deferred, so that it then receives no good which now evils sadden: and then is more fully swallowed up by punishments, which now rejoices in delights.
34.2: 34.2 Whom when Shechem had seen he lay with her, etc. AUGUSTINE, Questions on Genesis, vol. 3. And he set his mind on Dinah the daughter of Jacob and loved the maiden, and spoke according to the sense of the maiden. How is she called a maiden if he had already lain with her? Unless perhaps maiden is a name of age according to the Hebrew speech, or rather by recapitulation it is afterwards mentioned what was done before. For first he could set his mind on her soul and love the maiden and speak according to the sense of a maiden, then lie with her. Peaceful. Where the Septuagint interpreted peaceful, Aquila translated consummate and perfect, for which in the Hebrew is read: Shelemim. From which it appears that what we said above about Salem is true. They consented, etc. AUGUSTINE. A little before, Jacob, speaking with Esau, signifies that his sons were infants, etc., down to but his sons in this deed are named as chiefs and authors. Taking, etc. STRABO. So the pastors of the Church ought to avenge the sin of the flesh or the soul with the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God: ready to avenge all disobedience. We are few, etc. AUGUSTINE. He says this because wars might arise in great number, not that he had much less than would suffice for the storming of the city. Should they abuse our sister as a harlot? etc. AUGUSTINE. The zeal of the sons of Jacob in avenging their sister morally admonishes the pastors of the faithful to have care of the souls committed to them, lest they succumb to violent bodily fault or spiritual fornication. And let them be ready to avenge all disobedience, and strike the seducer with the sword of excommunication, lest he escape unpunished.
35.4: 35.4 They gave him therefore, etc. JEROME, Questions on Genesis, vol. 3. Plainly in this order and by these steps must one ascend to Bethel, that is to the house of God, which is the Church of Christ. The first is to renounce former errors and profess faith in the one true God, which is to put away strange gods: then to be baptized, which is to be cleansed; and thereafter to walk in newness of life, which is to change garments. The earrings signify the trappings of false doctrine, bright in speech but empty of the truth of sense. And the earrings, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked what sort of earrings, which were ornaments not pertaining to idolatry? But it must be understood that they were the phylacteries of strange gods.
35.6: 35.6 So Jacob came to Luz, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is to be noted that three names of this city are recorded, etc., down to for many reasons names are added or changed. JEROME. Behold it is most manifestly proved that Bethel was not called Ulam, as was said above, but Luz, that is almond, before.
35.10: 35.10 Your name shall not be called any more, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked, since it was once said, Your name shall not be called any more Jacob, etc., why he is afterwards read to be called Jacob? But this name belongs to that promise, in which God is seen as he was not before seen by the fathers, where there will be no old name: because nothing of the old man will remain in the body itself, and the vision of God will be the highest reward. JEROME. Your name shall not be called Jacob any more, etc. For not yet is the name imposed on him by the angel, but is foretold to be imposed by God. What is promised to be there in the future is here taught to be fulfilled.
35.11: 35.11 Increase and multiply. Morally. This promise belongs to the spiritual seed of Jacob, as was already said before of Abraham. For all who supplant vices and lay aside the old man with his deeds and fix the eyes of the mind on God, rightly belong to Jacob, whose faith and deeds they imitate. And kings shall come out of your loins, that is, the saints who according to the will of God truly rule themselves and their subjects: from whose spiritual seed, that is the imitation of faith, they become fruitful in good works.
35.14: 35.14 But he set up a pillar of stone in the place where God had spoken to him, etc. AUGUSTINE. What was done before was done again in this place; or what had been done before is here recorded. But whichever of these it be, Jacob poured a libation upon the stone, not to the stone. Not therefore as idolaters are wont to set altars before a stone and pour libations to the stone as to a god.
35.16: 35.16 Ephrath. JEROME. Ephrath and Bethlehem are the name of one city, with a similar interpretation. For it is interpreted fruitful and house of bread, on account of the bread that came down from heaven.
35.18: 35.18 And as her soul was departing, etc. ISIDORE. What does it mean that Rachel, when she bore him, called the same Benoni, son of my sorrow? Unless it be that from that tribe would come Paul, who would afflict the children of the Church in the time of his persecution? Otherwise by Benjamin is figured the earthly Jerusalem, which is in the tribe of Benjamin: whose people afflicted the mother with grievous sorrow by shedding the blood of the prophets, and by crying out for the death of Christ: His blood be upon us and upon our children, Matthew 27. And it came to pass when she was giving up the ghost. JEROME. Since she was dying she called his name, son of my sorrow: but his father called his name Benjamin. In the Hebrew the likeness of the name resounds, for son of my sorrow, the name the dying mother imposed, is Benoni. Son of the right hand, that is of power, which Jacob changed it to, is called Benjamin. Hence they err who think Benjamin is interpreted son of days: for the right hand is called yamin and ends in n; days is called yamim and ends in m.
35.21: 35.21 Departing thence, etc. JEROME. The Hebrews wish this place to be, etc., down to or what is truer, by a certain prophecy the mystery to come was already then shown.
35.22: 35.22 Reuben went, etc. ISIDORE. Allegorically. This crime would not be written unless the future perversity of the people were to be proclaimed: although in him it was a disgrace, in the Scriptures it is a prophecy of things to come, because by Reuben the firstborn the people of Israel is figured: who defiled the bed of the concubine, that is, stained the law of the Old Testament by transgressing it. That the concubine signified the Old Testament Paul shows, saying, Galatians 4: Abraham had two sons, one by a bondwoman, and the other by a free woman, etc. Now there were, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked how this is true, etc., down to than that it be taken by synecdoche.
35.27: 35.27 The city of Arba. JEROME. For Arba the Septuagint has plain, whereas Hebron is on a mountain. The same city in ancient times was called Mamre from a friend of Abraham. The city of Arba, etc. Of angels or holy souls, to whom he is added, no solicitude of temptations remaining, nor peril of sins.
36.6: 36.6 He went into another country. STRABO. It may be asked why Esau is said after his father's death to have gone into Seir and withdrawn from his brother, when already when Jacob came he is said to have dwelt in Seir? But it could be that when Jacob fled into Mesopotamia Esau, from grief at the blessing taken away, withdrew from his parent and dwelt in Seir for the twenty years Jacob was away. Reconciled to him on his return, he again came back from Seir and dwelt with his brother while his father lived: who being dead, he withdrew from his brother, because they were rich and could not dwell together.
36.20: 36.20 These are the sons of Seir, etc. JEROME in Hebrew Questions, vol. 3. After he has enumerated the sons of Esau, he repeats from further back who before Esau were chiefs in the land of Edom from the race of the Horites, which is interpreted free. In Deuteronomy it is written more clearly how the sons of Esau came, and the Horites being slain, inherited their land. The sons of Seir, etc. STRABO. That is the free, who, as is read in Paralipomenon, first dwelt in Mount Seir; who being driven out the Idumeans dwelt in their place.
36.22: 36.22 And the sister was, etc. JEROME. This is Timna, of whom it was said above: And Timna was concubine to Eliphaz, firstborn of Esau, etc. He therefore recalls the Horites because the firstborn of the sons of Esau took a concubine from their daughters. Because Teman, and Kenaz, and Amalek, and the rest are mentioned, let us know that afterwards the names of the regions and nations of the Idumeans were imposed from these.
36.24: 36.24 This is Anah, etc. STRABO. Some say simply that he found hot waters in the desert, which we call thermae. This is Anah, etc. JEROME. Various things are disputed among the Hebrews about this chapter, etc., down to that mules should be born against nature.
36.29: 36.29 These are the dukes. He says of the preceding, who are of Seir; not of these whom he begins to number, who are of Esau.
36.31: 36.31 And the kings. It is to be known that he does not mention all the kings who were before the sons of Israel had kings, the first of whom was Saul, but all these only who reigned before Moses died. And the kings. He mentions them according to the time in which the writer lived, but since Seir, who begot these, dwelt there, before Esau came into that land, it was called by him the land of Edom. AUGUSTINE, Questions on Genesis, vol. 3. It is no wonder that to those counting from Abraham through Esau the father of the nation of Edom, etc., down to for in that order where more are numbered they died sooner than here where fewer. Husham. JEROME. Whom some suspect to be Job, as is added at the end of that volume; but the Hebrews assert that he was begotten of the stock of Nahor, as was already said above.
37.2: 37.2 Joseph, when he was sixteen years old, etc. AUGUSTINE in Questions on Genesis. Historically. How can the death of Isaac, etc., down to yet Isaac living, Joseph began to be seventeen years old. And he was with the sons of Bilhah, etc. Joseph, one of the twelve sons of Jacob, beloved of his father above the others, signified Christ, whom God the Father preferred according to the flesh born over the other brethren begotten of the stock of Abraham. Hence Jacob loved him because he had begotten him in his old age. For the world growing old, the Son of God was born of the Virgin as a son of old age. And he was with, etc. In the primitive Church he did not cast off those who adhered to him through the preaching of the false apostles, whom the handmaids of Jacob signify, whom he also would not forbid when they worked miracles in his name.
37.3: 37.3 And he made him a coat of many colors. JEROME. For coat of many colors Aquila interpreted it as reaching to the ankles, Symmachus as sleeved, either because it descended to the ankles and was marked by the hands of the artist with a wonderful variety, or because it had sleeves: for the ancients used rather colobia, that is garments without sleeves. GREGORY, hom. XXV on the Gospels. Because Joseph is described as persevering just among his brethren to the end of his life, he alone is said to have had a coat to the ankles. What is the ankle-length coat but a consummated action? For as a stretched-out coat covers the heel of the body, so a good action governs us before the eyes of God to the end of life. Hence Moses commanded the tail of the victim to be offered, that the good work we begin we may complete with a persevering end.
37.4: 37.4 And his brethren seeing, etc. The brethren of Christ according to the flesh are the Jews, of whose kindred he took flesh. But because they saw that the grace of virtues was done in him, which testified the special love of the Father, they envied, nor could they speak to him anything peaceably, and more often attempted snares, and blasphemed that the Master of the house cast out demons in Beelzebub the prince of demons. ISIDORE. This was spiritually fulfilled in Christ, etc., down to in the figure of the stars.
37.10: 37.10 Shall I, etc. It may be asked according to the letter when he was adored by his father, who is meant by the sun; and by his mother, who is designated by the moon. For Jacob is not read to have adored him when he went down into Egypt: and the mother was already dead: but let us have recourse to the allegory, which is fulfilled in Christ.
37.12: 37.12 And when his brethren, etc., were feeding the flocks, down to Bring me word, etc. ISIDORE. Jacob sends his son to care for his brethren; and God the Father sends his only-begotten Son, to visit the human race languishing in sins. Hence Galatians chapter four: God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh. Joseph is sent to see if all things were prosperous with the sheep: and Christ says, Matthew fifteen: I was not sent but to the sheep that are lost of the house of Israel. In Dothan. Defection. For they were in great defection who were thinking of fratricide. Reuben. The prophetic word foreseeing this, which Reuben signifies, who is interpreted vision of the son, deterred with prophetic threats, that they might keep themselves innocent of the blood of Christ, their brother according to the flesh.
37.23: 37.23 They stripped him, etc. ISIDORE. Mystically. The Jews also stripped Christ by death of the bodily and many-colored coat, that is, adorned with the diversity of all the virtues. They sprinkled the coat with the blood of a kid: because accusing him by false testimonies they brought him to the odium of sin. Joseph is put into a cistern, that is into a pit: and Christ, stripped of human flesh, descended into hell.
37.25: 37.25 They saw travelers, Ishmaelites. AUGUSTINE. It is asked why Scripture Ishmaelites, etc., down to who say Hagar and Keturah were one?
37.28: 37.28 Drawing out. ISIDORE. Allegorically. Joseph lifted out of the cistern is sold to the Ishmaelites: and Christ returned from hell is purchased by the commerce of faith by all nations. He, by the counsel of Judah, is sold for thirty pieces of silver, and this one by the counsel of Judas Iscariot is sold for the same number. They sold. JEROME. The Hebrew truth has pieces of silver. For the Lord ought not to be sold for a cheaper metal than Joseph.
37.34: 37.34 And rending his garments, etc. ISIDORE. Jacob, weeping for the loss of his posterity, mourned as a father a lost son, and as a prophet the destruction of the Jews, Matthew 26. He rent his garment: which the chief priest did in the Lord's passion, Luke 23. But also the veil of the temple was rent, that it might prophesy his people stripped, and show the kingdom divided.
37.35: 37.35 I will go down to my son. etc. It is asked how this is to be understood, whether only the wicked or also the good go down into hell? If only the wicked, how does this man say that he in mourning wishes to go down to his son? For it is not credible that he is in the punishments of hell. Or are they the words of a disturbed and grieving man, exaggerating his woes even here? Or is it credible that in hell there were certain secret places, less penal, before the Lord's passion, to which even the saints went down? because none could enter paradise until Christ removed the fiery sword. JEROME. The Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar the eunuch, Pharaoh's chief cook. Scripture often puts chief cooks for masters of the army; in Greek mageiros is a cook, and it is derived from to kill: because cooks kill the beasts to be cooked. Joseph was therefore sold to the chief of the butchers, not Petephres, as is written in the Latin, but Potiphar the eunuch. Where it is asked how he is afterwards said to have a wife? The Hebrews hand down that Joseph was bought by him for the shameful ministry on account of his great beauty, and that by the master, his virility having withered, he was afterwards chosen, after the manner of the hierophants, that is those who speak sacred things, in the pontificate of Heliopolis: and that his daughter was Asenath, whom Joseph afterwards took as wife.
38.1: 38.1 At that time, etc. AUGUSTINE, Questions on Genesis. It is asked how these things could have happened? For if after Joseph came into Egypt, etc., down to that he fell in love with her whom he took to wife, Joseph not yet being sold. Judah, etc. He, like the other patriarchs, signifies Christ, who came down to the baptism of John. For Hirah is interpreted seeing God: Adullamite, witness in water, because John, seeing Christ coming to baptism, said: Behold the Lamb of God, etc., John 1. To this testimony the Synagogue adhered to Christ, which Shua, the daughter of the Canaanite, signifies, because to her was to be given the land of humble profession, which Canaan means. This Synagogue therefore first adhered to Christ, when Peter and Andrew and the other disciples of John became disciples of Christ. In what order these things were fulfilled the following history signifies, narrating how Judah went in to Tamar, which signifies the same as Shua.
38.3: 38.3 Who conceived, etc. The Synagogue begot rulers, who presided over her as husbands: of whom some were harmful, whom Er signifies, who is interpreted skinny, for skin signifies death, because the first parents clothed with skins were consigned to death; others useless, whom Onan signifies, who is interpreted their mourning, to whom, namely, they do not profit.
38.5: 38.5 She bore also a third, etc. ISIDORE on Genesis, vol. 5. The third son who is not joined to Tamar, etc., down to and therefore as an Adullamite he bore witness in water. Judah, etc. From Judah came the royal tribe, which long presided over the Jewish people, whom Tamar signifies, who is interpreted bitterness, because she showed herself bitter in the passion toward Christ. ISIDORE. The Jewish people, to whom the kings from the tribe of Judah, etc., down to yet God killed both, because he takes the kingdom away from such.
38.13: 38.13 To shear his sheep. STRABO. Allegorically. The Lord comes to shear the sheep, that is to unburden them of sins, of whom it is said: Your teeth are as flocks of sheep that are shorn. Tamar changes her garb: for Tamar is also interpreted changing; she changes garb and name, that from the Synagogue she may be the Church. But the name of bitterness remains: not that in which she ministered gall to the Lord, but that in which Peter wept bitterly. For Judah too is called Confession; let bitterness therefore be mingled with confession, that true penance may be prefigured. This penance is made fruitful, the Church being established in all nations. For it behooved Christ to suffer and to rise again, and that penance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations. The garb of a harlot is also the confession of sins: Tamar indeed signifies the Church called from the Gentiles; sitting in this garb at the gate of Enaim, which is interpreted fountain: because she ran like a hart to the fountains of waters, to come to the seed of Abraham. She is made fruitful by him not knowing, according to that of Psalm 17: A people whom I knew not has served me. She received in secret a ring, a bracelet, and a staff, because she is signed by calling, adorned by justification, exalted by glorification. Whom he predestined, them he also called; and whom he called, them he also justified, Romans 8; but in secret, where the conception of holy fruitfulness takes place.
38.14: 38.14 Who, laying aside the garments of her widowhood, etc. It is to be noted that even in the times of the patriarchs there were certain garments of widows, not such as those of married women. She sat in a crossroads. JEROME. And she sat at the gate of Enaim, which is on the way to Timnah. The Hebrew word, Enaim, is translated eyes. It is not therefore the name of a place, and the sense is, She sat in the crossroads, or at the junction, where the traveler ought to look more carefully where he goes.
